points.point: LLM judges inflate the benefit of personalisation: on a 1–5 preference scale where 3 is neutral, humans average 3.18 while all five LLM judges average higher, from 3.41 to 4.02.
points.paper: library/llm/personalization/methods/Re-Centering Humans in LLM Personalization.md
points.evidence: p. 15, Table 6: Human 3.176; Gemma-4-31B 3.409, Claude-S4.6 3.428, Qwen3.5-27B 3.487, GPT-5.4 3.523, Llama-3.3-70B 4.019. p. 8: 'humans assign lower ratings than all LLM judges'.

points.point: Judge–human item-level agreement is weak: Spearman with the human average rating is 0.11–0.38 across the five judges (at most 0.38).
points.paper: library/llm/personalization/methods/Re-Centering Humans in LLM Personalization.md

points.point: Humans rated 54.6% of personalised responses as no better than their generic counterparts.
points.paper: library/llm/personalization/methods/Re-Centering Humans in LLM Personalization.md
points.evidence: p. 8, §6.2: '54.6% of personalized responses are judged by humans as no better than their generic counterparts (rating ≤ 3.0)'.

points.point: Mechanism: several open-weight judges reward explicit mentions of a user attribute ('Given your interest in machine learning…'). Humans show almost no gap (Δ = 0.03), GPT-5.4 a small negative one (Δ = −0.07), and Claude Sonnet 4.6 over-penalises mentions (Δ = −0.39). The paper says such responses can feel robotic, presumptuous or intrusive to users.
points.paper: library/llm/personalization/methods/Re-Centering Humans in LLM Personalization.md
points.evidence: p. 8, §6.2 and Fig. 6: 'several open-weight judges assign higher scores to explicit mentions, while human annotators and GPT-5.4 show little sensitivity'; human Δ=0.03, Claude-S4.6 Δ=−0.39, GPT-5.4 Δ=−0.07; 'feel robotic, presumptuous, or intrusive to users'.

points.point: Models that mention user attributes more often as generators also reward such mentions more as judges: correlation 0.90 across five models (p = 0.04).
points.paper: library/llm/personalization/methods/Re-Centering Humans in LLM Personalization.md
points.evidence: p. 8, §6.2 and Fig. 7: 'strongly correlated (Spearman r=0.90, p=0.04)'. It is a Spearman correlation between a model's own mention rate and its own reward for mentions, across the five models.

points.point: Training does not fix it: reward models trained on the human ratings reach only about 0.3 Spearman with humans, comparable to the stronger LLM judges.
points.paper: library/llm/personalization/methods/Re-Centering Humans in LLM Personalization.md
points.evidence: p. 9, §6.3: ModernBERT, Qwen2.5-1.5B and Llama-3.2-1B reward models 'reach only around 0.3 Spearman correlation with human ratings. This is comparable to the stronger LLM judges ... such as Claude-S4.6 and GPT-5.4'.

points.point: The same gap appears one stage earlier, in deciding which user attributes are relevant to a prompt: humans mark about 20% of pairs relevant and LLMs 40–60%; LLM–human κ is 0.300, against 0.426 human–human and 0.597 LLM–LLM.
points.paper: library/llm/personalization/methods/Re-Centering Humans in LLM Personalization.md
points.evidence: p. 6, §5.2: human pairwise Cohen's κ 0.426, LLM–LLM 0.597, LLM–human 0.300; 'each human annotator marks only around 20% of attributes as relevant, whereas LLMs mark 40–60%'. Repeated on p. 15, Appendix G.

points.point: The human ceiling is low: the three annotators agree with each other at only Spearman 0.325 (weighted κ 0.310), so the best judges (0.36–0.38 against the human mean) are near the human–human level. The inflation and the mention bias are therefore the firmer findings (the answers' own reading).
points.paper: library/llm/personalization/methods/Re-Centering Humans in LLM Personalization.md
points.evidence: p. 8, §6.1 Human Annotation: inter-annotator agreement by 'Spearman correlation and weighted Cohen's κ, which gives 0.325 and 0.310'. The noise-ceiling reading is the answers' inference: the paper calls this 'reasonable annotator consistency' and still concludes that judges are unreliable substitutes.

points.point: The evidence is thin and uses third-party raters: Stage 3 rests on 80 items and 367 ratings from three Prolific annotators reading someone else's profile, not the users being personalised for.
points.paper: library/llm/personalization/methods/Re-Centering Humans in LLM Personalization.md
points.evidence: p. 15, Appendix G: 'A total of 80 items were annotated, producing 367 (item, attribute) ratings across three annotators'; 'Three human annotators participated in all annotation tasks ... recruited through Prolific'; they were shown 'a user's attribute profile, a prompt, and two responses'.

points.point: The paper's text and table disagree: the text says open-weight judges correlate very poorly and proprietary ones better, but Table 6 gives the highest correlation (0.376) to the open-weight Llama-3.3-70B, which is also the most inflated judge (4.02). So correlation alone does not pick a safe judge.
points.paper: library/llm/personalization/methods/Re-Centering Humans in LLM Personalization.md
points.evidence: p. 8: 'Open-weight judges show very low Spearman correlations with human ratings, while proprietary judges perform better, with the strongest reaching about 0.37.' p. 15, Table 6: Llama-3.3-70B has avg. rating 4.019 and Spearman 0.376, both the highest; Claude-S4.6 has 0.362 and GPT-5.4 0.312.

points.point: Synthetic users are easier than real ones, so benchmarks built on synthetic personas understate the difficulty.
points.paper: library/llm/personalization/methods/Re-Centering Humans in LLM Personalization.md
points.evidence: p. 4, §4.2 and Fig. 2: attributes extracted from real conversations have 'substantially higher proportions of uncertain and rejected cases' and 'synthetic data may underestimate the difficulty of this stage'. The paper shows this for attribute extraction (Stage 1) only, not for response judging.

points.point: LLM-simulated users (GPT-4o given each real participant's profile) recover the aggregate ranking of the systems: correlation with the human ranking is r = 0.98–0.99.
points.paper: library/llm/personalization/benchmarks/PRISM-X. Experiments on Personalised Fine-Tuning with Human and Simulated Users.md
points.evidence: p. 17, 'Aggregate hierarchies are recovered': Plackett–Luce worth parameters correlate at r=0.99 (Sim-Judgement) and r=0.98 (Sim-Dynamic). The study re-recruited 530 participants (p. 1); the simulation comparison uses 1,855 matched trials from 497 of them (p. 16), so both figures cited in the answers are in the paper.

points.point: The same simulators fall far below human self-consistency on individual judgements: per-trial Kendall τ 0.22 and 0.11 against 0.57, and top-1 accuracy 40.1% and 32.3% against 68.8%.
points.paper: library/llm/personalization/benchmarks/PRISM-X. Experiments on Personalised Fine-Tuning with Human and Simulated Users.md
points.evidence: p. 16–17, §4.1 and Fig. 8: human self-consistency ceiling τ=0.57, top-1 68.8%; Sim-Judgement τ=0.22 [0.20, 0.25], top-1 40.1%; Sim-Dynamic τ=0.11 [0.09, 0.14], top-1 32.3%.

points.point: Simulators have a much stronger position bias than humans: they rank the first-shown model best 44.9% of the time and the last 7.2% (33.8% and 15.0% in the other condition), while humans are near 25% for each position.
points.paper: library/llm/personalization/benchmarks/PRISM-X. Experiments on Personalised Fine-Tuning with Human and Simulated Users.md
points.evidence: p. 18, 'Simulators dramatically exacerbate UI position biases': humans A 24.1%, B 23.2%, C 24.1%, D 28.6%; Sim-Judgement A 33.8% vs D 15.0%; Sim-Dynamic A 44.9% vs D 7.2%. The two pairs quoted by different answers are the two conditions, so both are correct.

points.point: One simulation condition still swapped the top two models despite the near-perfect aggregate correlation.
points.paper: library/llm/personalization/benchmarks/PRISM-X. Experiments on Personalised Fine-Tuning with Human and Simulated Users.md
points.evidence: p. 17: 'Sim-Dynamic condition recovered the human ordering (PPFT > DPFT > Base > Prompting), but Sim-Judgement swapped the top two models, reversing the slim advantage for PPFT in the human study.'

points.point: The PRISM-X result is for a naive simulator (GPT-4o conditioned on a text persona), which the authors say is not the ceiling of what simulation can achieve. Simulated users were also far more sycophantic than real ones.
points.paper: library/llm/personalization/benchmarks/PRISM-X. Experiments on Personalised Fine-Tuning with Human and Simulated Users.md
points.evidence: Discussion: 'a widely-used but relatively naive paradigm (persona-conditioning via natural language in GPT-4o) rather than the ceiling of what more advanced methods can achieve'. p. 20: 'Real users almost never displayed sycophancy (90% scored 1/10)', human M=1.18 vs simulated M=3.41. p. 19 heading: 'Humans are more diverse than their simulated counterparts'.

points.point: Response length alone drives much of human preference: each additional 100 characters gives 1.57× the odds of being chosen, so length should be controlled for.
points.paper: library/llm/personalization/benchmarks/PRISM-X. Experiments on Personalised Fine-Tuning with Human and Simulated Users.md
points.evidence: p. 13, §3.4: 'each additional 100 characters was associated with 1.57× the odds of being chosen (p<.001)'. This is first-turn response length predicting the opening choice; for full-conversation length predicting ranked-best the odds ratio is 1.15.

points.point: Scoring against rubric aspects taken from the asker's own question narrative agrees with human annotators in 73% of cases, against 58% for direct scoring. The validation is small: 100 examples, two annotators, inter-annotator κ 0.726.
points.paper: library/llm/personalization/benchmarks/LaMP-QA. A Benchmark for Personalized Long-form Question Answering.md
points.evidence: p. 7, 'Effect of Evaluation Method and Auto-Rater Size': 100 test examples, each rated by two annotators, Cohen's κ 0.726; 'in 73% of cases, the aspect-based evaluation method selects the same response as human annotators, while the direct scoring method aligns ... in only 58%'.

points.point: Pairwise judging is order-dependent: the pairwise judge (Qwen 2.5, 32B) changed its preferred response in 78% of cases when the order of the two answers was reversed.
points.paper: library/llm/personalization/benchmarks/LaMP-QA. A Benchmark for Personalized Long-form Question Answering.md
points.evidence: p. 7: 'instruction-tuned Qwen 2.5 (32B parameters) changes its preferred response in 78% of cases when the order of the two responses is reversed.'

points.point: Small judges both agree less with humans and inflate scores: a 0.5B judge agrees 48% of the time with a mean score of 0.94, while a 32B judge agrees 73% with a mean score of 0.44.
points.paper: library/llm/personalization/benchmarks/LaMP-QA. A Benchmark for Personalized Long-form Question Answering.md
points.evidence: p. 7: 'with a 0.5B parameter model, alignment with human preferences is only 48%, and the average score assigned is relatively high at 0.94. In contrast, the 32B evaluator achieves a much higher alignment of 73% but assigns a significantly lower average score of 0.44.'

points.point: The most reliable evaluator of a personalised answer is the original user who asked the question; third-party annotators and judges are proxies.
points.paper: library/llm/personalization/benchmarks/LaMP-QA. A Benchmark for Personalized Long-form Question Answering.md
points.evidence: p. 10, Limitations, 'On the Automatic Evaluation of Personalization': 'the most reliable evaluator is the original user who posed the question. However, consistently obtaining feedback from the same user ... is impractical, costly, and in many cases impossible.' Verified for LaMP-QA only; some answers attribute the same statement to Re-Centering Humans, which was not checked.

points.point: Personalisation is the judge's weakest dimension: judge–human κ is 0.52 on personalisation against 0.78 on task completion, while human annotators agree among themselves at 0.75 and 0.865. The validation is 100 dialogues with three annotators.
points.paper: library/llm/personalization/benchmarks/PersonaLens. A Benchmark for Personalization Evaluation in Conversational AI Assistants.md
points.evidence: p. 8, §4.7 and Table 5: Task Completion Cohen's κ 0.780 / Fleiss IAA 0.865; Personalization 0.520 / 0.750. 0.520 is the lowest judge–human κ of the six metrics; 100 sampled dialogues, three annotators.

points.point: For binary checks against a stated preference (violated, acknowledged, hallucinated, helpful), the Claude 3 Sonnet judge agrees with humans at 86–98% per checker and 0.92–0.97 on final preference-following accuracy.
points.paper: library/llm/personalization/benchmarks/Do LLMs Recognize Your Preferences. Evaluating Personalized Preference Following in LLMs.md
points.evidence: p. 43, §A.17, Table 18: checker agreement ranges from 0.86 (Violate, implicit choice-based) to 0.98 (Hallucinate, explicit); Preference Following Accuracy 0.97 / 0.92 / 0.96; 100 sampled evaluations per preference form.

points.point: For checklist-based matching of an inferred preference to the ground truth, the GPT-4o judge reaches Krippendorff α = 0.769 against the human majority vote, and a distilled 7B matcher 0.748.
points.paper: library/llm/personalization/benchmarks/CUPID. Evaluating Personalized and Contextualized Alignment of LLMs from Interactions.md
points.evidence: p. 3, §2.3 'Inference - Preference Match': 'GPT-4o achieved a Krippendorff's alpha of 0.769 (substantial agreement) with the majority vote of human annotators ... PrefMatcher-7B ... 0.748'. The figure is on p. 3, not p. 8 as some answers cite. The appendix reports α 0.467 between the human annotators themselves.

points.point: The LLM judge aligns with human experts at 73–96% depending on the task, across four memory and preference tasks.
points.paper: library/llm/personalization/benchmarks/AlpsBench. An LLM Personalization Benchmark for Real-Dialogue Memorization and Preference Alignment.md
points.evidence: §3 (p. 4), 'LLM-as-a-Judge Alignment' and Fig. 5: 'alignment rates of 96% for Task 3, 85% for Task 2, 83% for Task 4, and 73% for Task 1'.

points.point: For over-personalisation metrics (irrelevance, sycophancy), judge scores correlate with human scores at Spearman about 0.60–0.74 across judge models: 0.68 for the GPT-4o-mini judge actually used, 0.74 for the best.
points.paper: library/llm/personalization/benchmarks/OP-Bench. Benchmarking Over-Personalization for Memory-Augmented Personalized Conversational Agents.md
points.evidence: p. 14, §A.3.2, Table 5: Spearman ρ from 0.61/0.60 (DeepSeek-v3.2) to 0.74/0.74 (Claude-Opus-4.5-thinking) for irrelevance/sycophancy; GPT-4o-mini 0.68/0.68, chosen as the judge; 100 queries, 200 responses. Answer G's '0.62–0.71' understates the range.

points.point: Given the user's true rubric, a judge picks the right response almost perfectly (97.5% directional agreement with humans on 2,830 pairs; oracle accuracy 97.8–99.1%), but the best model reaches only about 76% (75.94%) when it has to infer the needs itself. The pairs were built to follow or violate the rubric, so the first case is easy by construction.
points.paper: library/llm/post-training/preference-learning/Personalized RewardBench. Evaluating Reward Models with Human Aligned Personalization.md
points.evidence: p. 17, §B.4: 'directional agreement reaches 97.5% (2,758 / 2,830)', 99.7% excluding ties. p. 15, §B.1: oracle Gemini-3-Flash with ground-truth rubric aspects scores 97.78%, 99.09% and 98.60%, against a state-of-the-art peak of 75.94%. p. 6, §4.2: the best model 'fails to surpass the 76% accuracy threshold'. Abstract: pairs are built 'based on strict adherence to (or violation of) user-specific rubrics'.

points.point: Small (8B-class) LLM judges pass generic answers off as personalised, scoring 0–19% accuracy on the correct-but-generic class, where a small entailment model does far better. The LLM judges still do better at identifying the personalised class.
points.paper: library/llm/personalization/methods/Evaluating LLM Personalization via Semantic Constraint Verification.md
points.evidence: p. 7, §4.3, Table 3: accuracy on the Generalized class is Qwen3-8B 18.69%, DeepSeek-R1 0.00%, Llama-3-8B 0.00%, Falcon-H1R 3.09%, against DeBERTa-Large 93.23%; overall mean 68.44% against 27–33% for the LLM judges. On the Personalized class DeBERTa-Large gets 43.50%, below Llama-3-8B (61.68%) and DeepSeek-R1 (46.25%). This is what the table shows; whether the text explicitly concedes it was not checked.

points.point: The judge can pick a different winner from humans: GPT-4 as judge puts P-Soups first on average pairwise win rate, while human judges put P-MORL first.
points.paper: library/llm/personalization/methods/Personalized Soups. Personalized Large Language Model Alignment via Post-hoc Parameter Merging.md
points.evidence: p. 7, §4.3, Tables 3–4: under GPT-4, P-Soups averages 55.23%; under human evaluation P-MORL averages 58.70% against 55.29% for P-Soups. The text notes 'a discrepancy between the simulated and human evaluation; P-Soups has the highest average win rate in GPT-4'.

points.point: When a judge is calibrated to abstain on low-confidence items, the abstained items are the ones humans also find subjective: human inter-annotator agreement is 0.815 on abstained samples against 0.902 on evaluated ones. The agreement guarantee therefore covers only the easier items.
points.paper: library/llm/evaluation/methods/Trust or Escalate. LLM Judges with Provable Guarantees for Human Agreement.md
points.evidence: p. 7, §3.3, Table 4: Human IAA 0.815 (abstained) vs 0.902 (evaluated), p < 1e-8; 'instances abstained by LLM judges tend to be more subjective even for humans'. Measured on ChatArena, not on personalisation data.

points.point: An LLM judge rated the PUMA system's responses above those of real human counsellors (average 4.37 against 3.85).
points.paper: library/llm/personalization/user-modelling/Know You Before You Speak. User-State Modeling for LLM Personalization in Multi-Turn Conversation.md
points.evidence: p. 7, §5.2 'Counselor-side MI quality', Table 2: LLM-judge MITI average is 3.85 for 'Real (human)' and 4.37 for PUMA (4.27 with the second backbone). The paper describes PUMA as 'comparable to the human-reference responses' and has no human validation of the judge. This is a 31st point, kept because it checks out; drop it if the cap of 30 is strict.

errors.quote: both Re-Centering Humans and LaMP-QA say the user is the only real authority
errors.paper_says: Only LaMP-QA says this: "the most reliable evaluator is the original user who posed the question" (Limitations, p. 10). Re-Centering Humans has no such statement; it argues for grounding evaluation in human data and judgments (§3, p. 3), and its Limitations (p. 9) say only that different users may reasonably prefer different forms of adaptation.

nonotes-q3-r2.comment: Table 6 values, the PrefEval, RewardBench, LaMP-QA and PersonaLens figures, the PRISM-X figures (497 participants, r = 0.99, τ 0.22 vs 0.57, 33.8%/15.0% position bias) and all page links check out. Point 27 is counted on the 97.5% and the easy-by-construction caveat; the 76% half is missing. Point 14 is given with the Sim-Judgement numbers only. The answer says openly that Prediction-Powered Inference and Trust or Escalate were not re-read; that is not reliance on a review or note.

errors.paper_says: OP-Bench Table 5 (A.3.2, p. 14) gives Spearman ρ from 0.60 (DeepSeek-v3.2: 0.61 irrelevance, 0.60 sycophancy) to 0.74 (Claude-Opus-4.5-thinking). The GPT-4o-mini judge is at 0.68.

errors.quote: No paper in the library has users rate answers to their own questions, so the real target is untested.
errors.paper_says: PRISM-X does this: 530 re-recruited participants chose and ranked four models in their own conversations (abstract, p. 1; Fig. 1 caption), and §4.1 (p. 16–17) scores the simulators against those participants' own rankings. The answer itself cites this study.

errors.quote: Simulated twins of 530 real participants recover the aggregate ranking of four models
errors.paper_says: Minor: the simulated-versus-human comparison uses 1,855 matched trials from 497 participants (§4.1, p. 16). 530 is the number recruited for the human study.

asis-q3-r3.review_only: This figure is from the library's note on the paper; I did not reopen the paper.
asis-q3-r3.misleading: Slightly: the closing claim that the real target is untested ignores that PRISM-X compares against the users' own rankings. The main verdict (no replacement; usable for stated criteria and aggregate ranking) matches the papers.
asis-q3-r3.comment: Point 10 is counted for 'best-correlated judge is also the most inflated, so correlation does not pick a safe judge'; the answer does not mention that the paper's text and table disagree. Point 26 is counted although the range is misquoted. The 0.40 human-versus-others figure is labelled as the answer's own calculation and is arithmetically right from 0.325. The claim about failing to write to reviews/ could not be checked.

errors.quote: Judges reward explicit mentions of the profile ("Given your interest in ML…").
errors.paper_says: Only "several open-weight judges" do (§6.2, p. 8, Fig. 6). GPT-5.4 shows little sensitivity (Δ = −0.07) and Claude-S4.6 significantly penalises explicit mentions (Δ = −0.39).

errors.quote: tests GPT-4o simulated users that have the profile, against 530 real users
errors.paper_says: Minor: the simulated-versus-human comparison uses 1,855 matched trials from 497 participants (§4.1, p. 16). 530 is the number recruited for the human study.

noreviews+claude-sonnet-5-5-q3-r1.review_only: I read the library's notes on this, not the full papers, so page numbers come from those notes.
noreviews+claude-sonnet-5-5-q3-r1.comment: The numbers hold in the papers despite the answer being built from notes: PrefEval 0.92–0.97 (p. 43), CUPID 0.769/0.748 (p. 3), Trust or Escalate 0.815/0.902 (p. 7), PRISM-X 1.57× (p. 13), and Reliability without Validity κ 0.511 against exact match 0.849 (p. 4). The Coin Flip figure is 13.6% (13.3% and 13.9% per judge, p. 7) on deliberately competitive pairs, so '13% on near-tied pairs' is acceptable. Point 4 is counted without the human Δ; point 14 without numbers; point 16 on the sycophancy half only. OP-Bench is named but not cited.

errors.quote: Same pairs, but inferring the needs from the user's history | best model about 76%
errors.paper_says: The 75.94% is obtained without the user's history: "Unless otherwise noted, we exclude the user profile u from the reward model input" (§4.1, p. 6), and §4.3 (p. 7) discusses profiles separately. The models infer the needs from the query and response alone.

nonotes-q3-r3.comment: All other numbers and page links check out, including 44.9%/7.2% (Sim-Dynamic, p. 18), τ 0.22 against 0.57 and 40% against 68.8% (p. 17), and the naive-simulator caveat (p. 25). Point 9 is counted without the 367 ratings; point 16 on the naive-simulator half only; point 27 without the easy-by-construction caveat.

errors.quote: Six papers in the library bear on this; only one tests the second question directly.
errors.paper_says: The answer itself draws on eight library papers that bear on the question (Re-Centering Humans, PRISM-X, PrefEval, CUPID, AlpsBench, OP-Bench, LaMP-QA, PersonaLens) and names two more, so the count of six is wrong.

nonotes-q3@run1.comment: Widest coverage, and every number and page link checked holds: AlpsBench 73–96% (p. 4), CUPID 0.769 (p. 3), OP-Bench 0.60–0.74 (p. 14), LaMP-QA 48%/0.94 against 73%/0.44 (p. 7), and Re-Centering 0.325 (p. 8). Points 12 and 13 are stated in words without numbers, from the PRISM-X abstract only, which the answer discloses. It also says it checked only the summaries of Prediction-Powered Inference and Trust or Escalate; that is a disclosed limit, not reliance on a review or note. Papers cited counts those two, which are named without links.

asis-q3@run1.review_only: This comes from the [personalisation review](reviews/llm/personalization.md) and the notes on the two real-user studies; I did not reopen the papers.
asis-q3@run1.comment: Every number and page I checked matches the papers (54.6% and Fig. 5 on p. 8; 3.41–4.02 vs 3.18 and ρ ≤ 0.38 in Table 6, p. 15; r = 0.90; PRISM-X r = 0.98–0.99, τ 0.22/0.11 vs 0.57; SCV 0–19% in Table 3, p. 7; LaMP-QA 78%, p. 7; PersonaLens 0.78/0.52; 80 items and 367 ratings, p. 15). The answer says outright that it rests on a review and notes and was not checked in the papers; the PersonaLens point is also flagged as 'from a skim-level digest, no page'. The 'κ 0.31–0.43' range mixes Stage 3 (weighted κ 0.310) with Stage 2 (κ 0.426) without saying so. Point 4 is stated only as the mechanism (judges reward explicit mentions), without the human/GPT-5.4/Claude contrast. 'No paper in the library has users judge answers to their own questions over time' is borderline, since PRISM-X participants do rate responses in their own conversations; I did not count it because of the 'over time' qualifier.

asis-q3-r2.comment: All checked statements hold: Fig. 6 reading (open-weight judges reward mentions, humans and GPT-5.4 little sensitivity, Claude-S4.6 negative), Table 6 on p. 15, PRISM-X τ and r, PersonaLens Table 5 on p. 8 (0.52/0.75, 0.78/0.865, 100 dialogues), LaMP-QA 73%/58%/κ 0.726/78% on p. 7, Personalized Soups Tables 3–4 on p. 7 (P-Soups 55.23 under GPT-4, P-MORL 58.70 under humans), reward models about 0.3 on p. 9, inter-annotator 0.325/0.310 on p. 8, best judges 0.31–0.38. The skipped-paper claim is correct (catalog/skipped.yaml: arXiv 2406.11657, 2026-10-01, 'narrow'). The mention of the evaluation review is a how-to pointer, not evidence for a point. The claim that no paper has users rate their own answers 'over time' and compares a judge against that is borderline given PRISM-X, which the answer itself describes as the closest test; not counted as an error.

noreviews-q3-r2.comment: Broadest and fully accurate on everything I checked: Re-Centering Table 6 (p. 15), §6.3 (p. 9), §6.2 (p. 8), §5.2 (p. 6; κ 0.300/0.426/0.597 rounded); CUPID α 0.769 on 230 items (p. 3); LaMP-QA 73%/58%, 78%, 48%/0.94 vs 73%/0.44 (p. 7) and the original-user statement (p. 10); RewardBench oracle 97.78–99.09% (p. 15) vs 75.94%, and rejected responses 'generated deliberately to avoid these criteria' (p. 4); PersonaLens Table 5; OP-Bench 0.68 for GPT-4o-mini and 0.74 for the best judge (A.3.2, p. 14); AlpsBench 73–96% (p. 4); PRISM-X r, τ, top-1 and 44.9%/7.2% (p. 18); Trust or Escalate abstention (p. 7). The Prediction-Powered Inference paper indeed has no LLM-judge experiment, and the answer says that use is by analogy. The position-bias figure quoted is the Sim-Dynamic condition only, not labelled as such. Omits 54.6%, the text/table inconsistency and the naive-simulator caveat.

nonotes-q3-r1.comment: No errors found. Checked: 54.6% (p. 8), Table 6, r = 0.90, Δ = 0.03 and −0.39, reward models about 0.3 (p. 9), κ 0.60/0.30 and 20% vs 40–60% (p. 6), PRISM-X τ 0.22, 40.1% vs 0.57, 68.8% (p. 17) and 33.8%/15.0% (p. 18), RewardBench 97.5% on 2,830 pairs (B.4, p. 17), LaMP-QA 73%/58% and judge sizes, PersonaLens (personalisation is the lowest of the six rows in Table 5), 80 items/367 ratings/three annotators (Appendix G, p. 15), the text-vs-Table 6 inconsistency (Llama-3.3-70B: 0.376 and 4.019), the naive-simulator caveat (p. 25), and Beyond Recall's 'feasible … but was not done' (§3.3, p. 23). Point 12 is stated without the r value; point 13 only for the Sim-Judgement condition; point 27 without the ~76% inferred-needs figure; point 16 without the sycophancy half. It is the only answer to catch point 10. It says it did not reread PPI and Trust or Escalate, which are named only as pointers.

errors.quote: No paper here has users rate answers to their own requests. The human raters are third parties reading a profile, so even the "human" side is a proxy
errors.paper_says: PRISM-X, which the answer itself cites, is first-party: 530 re-recruited participants each conversed with all four models blind and gave their own ratings, rankings and willingness-to-pay bids (Introduction, p. 2; §3.1 Protocol, p. 8), and the simulators are scored against those participants' own rankings (§4.1, p. 16–17).

errors.quote: both Re-Centering and LaMP-QA say the user is the only reliable judge
errors.paper_says: Only LaMP-QA says something close, and weaker: 'the most reliable evaluator is the original user who posed the question' (Limitations, p. 10). Re-Centering Humans makes no such statement; its Limitations (p. 9) say only that personalisation is subjective and that averaging collapses variation across annotators.

CUPID does give the human ceiling for this meta-evaluation: agreement between the three annotators is Krippendorff's α 0.467, 'moderate agreement' (Appendix A.1, Meta-Evaluation for Preference Match, p. 15). The judge's 0.769 is against the majority vote.

asis-q3-r1.misleading: Mildly: the conclusion (no for 'better for this person', yes for rubric checks) is sound, but saying no paper has users rate answers to their own requests hides that PRISM-X is exactly that first-party evidence, so a reader would underrate how directly the individual-level failure is established.
asis-q3-r1.comment: Numbers and pages are otherwise accurate: Table 6 (p. 15), 0.325 ceiling, PRISM-X τ 0.22 vs 0.57 and 40.1% vs 68.8% (p. 17, Fig. 8), r = 0.98–0.99, PersonaLens Table 5 (Fleiss κ 0.75), LaMP-QA 73%/58%/κ 0.726/78%/48%–73%/0.94–0.44, CUPID α 0.769 (p. 3), 54.6% (p. 8), reward models about 0.3 (p. 9), SCV 0–19% (Table 3, p. 7) and its concession in Limitations (p. 9) that LLM judges are still ahead on identifying the personalised class. The skipped-paper claim is correct. The mention of the review file is about a failed write, not evidence.

asis+claude-sonnet-5-5-q3-r1.review_only: I took these from the library's review and haven't re-read the papers
asis+claude-sonnet-5-5-q3-r1.comment: No wrong numbers or pages found; the Re-Centering and PRISM-X figures and pages all check out. Two overstatements that stop short of errors: 'Judges reward visible personalising' is said of judges in general, while the paper (p. 8) limits it to several open-weight judges, with GPT-5.4 showing little sensitivity and Claude-S4.6 a negative gap. And the opening 'A judge can rank systems against each other' rests only on PRISM-X's simulated users, where Sim-Judgement swapped the top two models (p. 17). Four points (Semantic Constraint Verification, LaMP-QA 78%, PersonaLens, PUMA) are openly flagged as taken from the review, though the numbers match the papers. The line 'No paper here has users rate answers to their own questions over time' is defensible only because of 'over time': PRISM-X does have the users themselves rate.

errors.quote: CUPID ([p. 8](...CUPID...pdf?page=8)) | Match inferred preference to ground truth via checklists | α = 0.769 vs human majority
errors.paper_says: The α = 0.769 meta-evaluation of the GPT-4o matcher is in §2.3 Metrics, 'Inference - Preference Match (p. 3)'. Page 8 holds only the PrefMatcher-7B vs GPT-4o correlation and the generation-task results; 0.769 appears nowhere else in the paper.

noreviews-q3-r3.review_only: I took the Personalized RewardBench figures from a skim-level digest
noreviews-q3-r3.comment: The numbers are accurate throughout; the only error is the CUPID page. The RewardBench figures it flags as coming from a digest are nonetheless correct (Table 2 on p. 6, oracle bound in B.1 on p. 15, best model 75.94%). It marks the noise-ceiling argument as its own reading. Point 14 is given only for the Sim-Dynamic condition and without the human ~25% baseline. Point 30 is stated without the agreement numbers, but the Table 4, p. 7 citation is right.

noreviews-q3-r1.comment: No errors found. It is the only answer with the right CUPID page (p. 3). 'Two open-weight judges were below 0.2' matches Table 6 (Qwen3.5 0.182, Gemma-4 0.111). PersonaLens and CUPID do use synthetic users, and Prediction-Powered Inference and Trust or Escalate are both in the library. The opening claim that even on rubric checks the judge 'agrees with humans less than humans agree with each other' is shown only for PersonaLens (0.520 vs 0.750); CUPID and LaMP-QA do not give a comparable pair, so it is a generalisation from one paper. It omits the 54.6% figure, the r = 0.90 generator–judge link and the reward-model result.

errors.quote: CUPID | Does the inferred preference match the ground truth, by checklist? | α = 0.769 (p. 8)
errors.paper_says: The α = 0.769 agreement with the human majority vote is reported in §2.3 Metrics, 'Inference - Preference Match (p. 3)', not on p. 8.

noreviews-q3@run1.comment: Widest coverage, and accurate apart from the CUPID page. Checked and correct: PrefEval 0.92–0.97 (A.17, Table 18, p. 43), AlpsBench 73–96% (p. 4, Fig. 5), OP-Bench 0.68 / 0.74 (A.3.2, Table 5, p. 14), PersonaLens 0.52 vs 0.78 (p. 8, Table 5), synthetic easier than real (p. 4). The PrefEval row is labelled 'Did the response violate a stated preference?', but 0.92–0.97 is the final preference-following accuracy row; the violation checker itself is 0.86–0.95. I did not count this as an error because the range quoted is a real row of the same table. It claims to have added a Q&A entry to notes/; this copy of the library has no notes/ directory, so I could not confirm that write.

errors.quote: PersonaMem-v3 audits its data with LLM judges only
errors.paper_says: The PersonaMem-v3 data-quality verification section reports automated quality filters and a GPT-5.5 judge re-evaluation (96.6% pass rate), but also says "we also conduct qualitative human inspection ourselves to identify subtle data-quality issues and artifacts, iterating over a hundred of times". So the audit is not LLM-only; what is absent is a human study of judge accuracy.

errors.quote: A judge at 0.38 is therefore not far below the raters' own agreement
errors.paper_says: Minor, wrong direction: Re-Centering Humans gives inter-annotator Spearman 0.325 (p. 8) and the best judge 0.376 against the human average (p. 15, Table 6). The best judge is numerically above the human-human figure, not below it (the two are not like for like).

errors.quote: Spearman 0.61–0.74 across eleven judges on 200 responses
errors.paper_says: Minor: OP-Bench Table 5 (p. 14) gives 0.61–0.74 for Irrelevance only; Sycophancy runs 0.60–0.74 (DeepSeek-v3.2 = 0.60). The row is labelled as the over-personalisation score in general, so the range is 0.60–0.74. Eleven judges and 200 responses are correct.

asis-v2-q3-r2.review_only: its note records no human study of judge accuracy
asis-v2-q3-r2.comment: Broadest coverage of the three, and the only one to state the top-two swap (15) and CUPID (24). Pages and numbers check out for Re-Centering, PRISM-X, PersonaLens, LaMP-QA, CUPID and Semantic Constraint Verification. Points counted leniently: 4 has no deltas and no Claude over-penalisation; 9 has no 367 ratings or Prolific; 14 gives 33.8%/15.0% without the human ~25% baseline; 13 gives only the Sim-Judgement condition. The PersonaMem-v3 line leans on a note rather than the paper and is partly wrong. The library-wide claims ('Only PRISM-X has the person being personalised for do the judging', 'Nothing in the library has users judge answers ... over time') were not checked.

asis-v2-q3-r1.review_only: The calibration advice comes from the evaluation review's "Calibrating the judge against people" section; I did not re-read its source papers.
asis-v2-q3-r1.comment: No wrong statement found; every number and page I checked holds: Re-Centering p. 6 (κ 0.300/0.426/0.597, 20% vs 40–60%), p. 8, p. 9 and p. 15 Table 6; PersonaLens Table 5 including 0.865; LaMP-QA p. 7 and p. 10; PRISM-X p. 16–17; Semantic Constraint Verification Table 3 and p. 9; HorizonBench p. 7 (56–64% majority-vote accuracy); and the skipped.yaml entry for 'Can LLM be a Personalized Judge?' (2406.11657, reason says narrow). The only answer to cover Stage 2 relevance matching (7). The OP-Bench range '0.60–0.68 for the five judges I read' is literally true of the first five rows and openly hedged, but understates the table (eleven judges, best 0.74); counted as 26 leniently. Omits 54.6%, the reward-model result, judge-size inflation and position bias. 9 counted on 'three third-party raters on 80 items'. The practical advice (calibrate on a few hundred human labels) is flagged as resting on a review, not checked in papers.

asis-v2-q3-r3.review_only: its line that LLM judges call generic answers personalised (Semantic Constraint Verification) rests on 8B-class judges. [...] I did not re-read its Table 3.
asis-v2-q3-r3.comment: No wrong statement found. Verified: PrefEval p. 43 Table 18 (0.92–0.97 is the final-accuracy row; per-checker is 0.86–0.98); OP-Bench Table 5 (0.68 GPT-4o-mini, 0.74 best); PersonaLens Table 5; Re-Centering p. 8 (54.6%, Δ 0.03 and −0.39), p. 9 and p. 15 (80 items, 367 ratings, 3.41–4.02 vs 3.18); LaMP-QA p. 7 and p. 10; PRISM-X p. 16–18 (44.9% vs 7.2% is the Sim-Dynamic condition). The only answer with PrefEval (23) and with the full point 4 deltas. 14 counted leniently (no human ~25% baseline); 28 counted leniently: it gives the claim and the limitation (p. 9) but no 0–19% figure, attributes the claim to the review, and says Table 3 was not re-read. That sits slightly at odds with 'every number below was checked in the paper itself', though no unchecked number is actually quoted.
